Solvent

SOL-vent -- built on the root '-solv-,' meaning to loosen or release, here used in its financial sense. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Solvent is having enough money to pay all of one's debts; not bankrupt.

After years of careful budgeting, the family-owned shop finally became completely solvent.

Worked Example

A small business owner spends two years aggressively paying down loans, cutting unnecessary costs, and rebuilding cash reserves until the company's bank account finally shows more assets than debts.

That financial state of being able to cover every debt owed is exactly what solvent means here. Unlike 'wealthy,' which implies having a lot of money, solvent simply means one's debts don't exceed one's assets.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

sound: Sound describes finances that are secure and dependable with room to spare -- strong enough to absorb a bad year. A business can be solvent and still fragile: solvent only means it can cover what it owes today.

creditworthy: Creditworthy means a lender judges you safe to lend to -- a question about the future and about new debt. Solvent is about the present: your assets already cover every debt you currently owe.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

insolvent: unable to pay one's debts

bankrupt: legally declared unable to pay one's debts

Where it sits · how fully anything owed is covered — stable → solvent → debt-free

stable vs. solvent: Stable is a broader financial term than solvent -- stable can describe steady income or manageable expenses generally, while solvent specifically means one's assets are enough to cover every debt owed.

debt-free vs. solvent: Debt-free can sound even stronger than solvent: solvent simply means debts can be paid off, while debt-free means no debts exist at all.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — solv-

root — solv-: to loosen, to release (Latin (solvere))

suffix — -ent

suffix — -ent: doing or being; forms an adjective (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Latin solvere meant 'to loosen or release,' and the suffix -ent forms the adjective. To be solvent is to be released from debt -- loosened from financial obligation by having enough to pay it off.

Use the root in a new word: resolve

Use the root in a new word: resolve: The two neighbors finally sat down together to resolve their long-running dispute over the fence.
